strengths: Large-scale, carefully documented pretraining pipeline using exclusively open CT datasets (229,619 series across 8 sources), with detailed preprocessing, filtering, and hardware description that supports reproducibility.

Reasonably well-motivated architectural adaptation to the specific challenges of volumetric CT (token scaling, anisotropy, geometry) via a two-stage local/global ViT design with 3D RoPE and DINOv3-style jittering, and a principled adaptation of SigLIP for many-to-many clinical text supervision.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning three distinct task families (frozen-embedding biomarker classification across 6 datasets and 11 competing foundation models, semantic segmentation across 4 datasets, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on 2 datasets), which is more extensive than most concurrent CT foundation model papers.

Encoder-only segmentation protocol (SEoMT) is a clean way to isolate representation quality from decoder engineering, and the paper is transparent about its limitations (loss of fine detail from 1/4-resolution prediction).

Reasonably honest discussion of limitations (thoracic data skew, weaker abdominal performance, noisy report supervision) and inclusion of failure cases/ablations (e.g., optimizer and crop-size ablations, saliency maps, UMAP visualizations) rather than only favorable results.
Public release of training code and pretraining recipes is promised, which could benefit the community given costly compute requirements.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily integrative rather than fundamental: the core components (DINOv3 SSL, SigLIP alignment, 3D RoPE, EoMT-style segmentation head) are directly adapted from existing 2D/3D methods, with limited new methodological contribution beyond engineering choices (windowing, local/global hierarchy) that are not deeply ablated against simpler alternatives (e.g., no ablation isolating the benefit of the two-stage local/global attention scheme itself, or of omitting the Gram loss, versus single-stage baselines).

Pretraining corpus (229K series) is substantially larger than most compared baselines (e.g., FMCIB ~11K, CT-CLIP ~25K, Merlin ~15K), confounding claims that architectural/algorithmic choices rather than data scale drive the reported gains; no controlled scaling comparison is provided.

The abstract's claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' is not fully supported by the results: it loses to Merlin substantially on Findings-based retrieval (Table 3), loses to nnU-Net ResEnc L on KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD segmentation (Table 1), and does not achieve top performance on 2 of 6 biomarker tasks (Fig. 1/3), making the overall framing somewhat overstated relative to the mixed empirical picture.

Several architectural hyperparameters (embedding dimension 1080, G=36 windows, specific patch sizes) appear to be fixed choices without ablation or justification beyond intuition, limiting insight into which design decisions actually matter.

No code/model link is actually provided in the submission (footnote is empty), and reproducibility relies entirely on a promise of future release, which cannot be independently verified at review time.

Statistical comparison is inconsistent across experiments: confidence intervals are reported for biomarker classification but not for segmentation or retrieval results, making it hard to assess whether reported margins (often <1-2 Dice points or moderate recall differences) are meaningful.

strengths: Large-scale, fully open pretraining corpus (~230K CT series from only public datasets) and release of code/recipes would be valuable to the community if delivered as promised.

Reasonably comprehensive downstream evaluation spanning biomarker classification (6 datasets, 11 baselines), semantic segmentation (4 datasets), and cross-modal retrieval (2 datasets), using established third-party protocols (TumorImagingBench, nnU-Net, EoMT) for fairer comparison.

The local/global ViT decomposition with window-level and scan-level tokens, combined with 3D RoPE and DINOv3-style box jittering, is a sensible and clearly described engineering response to the token-scaling problem in volumetric transformers.
Some useful ablations are reported (optimizer choice, crop size, SSL vs. SSL+VLA initialization) that could help practitioners replicate training.
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (thoracic data skew, smoothed segmentation outputs, reliance on noisy reports).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core ingredients (DINOv3 SSL, SigLIP VLA, EoMT-style encoder-only segmentation, windowed/hierarchical 3D attention, 3D RoPE) are all directly borrowed from prior work with only modest, largely engineering-level adaptations (patch anisotropy, jittered RoPE scale, two-stage local/global token aggregation); the paper's own related-work section already lists several very similar windowed/hierarchical 3D transformer designs, undercutting the originality claim.

The headline claim that SPECTRE "consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models" is not well supported by the actual results: on segmentation it underperforms the strongest conventional baseline (nnU-Net / nnU-Net ResEnc L) on 3 of 4 datasets (KiTS23, LiTS, WORD) and loses to nnU-Net on AMOS-CT; on retrieval, Merlin substantially outperforms SPECTRE on Findings-to-image retrieval (e.g., 77.6 vs 55.5 Recall@1 at N=32), a fairly large gap that is downplayed in the discussion.

The main quantitative result for the flagship biomarker benchmark is presented only as a radar plot (Fig. 1) in the main text, without a corresponding numerical table, making it hard to assess exact magnitudes of improvement or losses relative to baselines directly in the paper body (numbers only appear via a supplementary bar chart with wide confidence intervals).

Ablation studies justifying key architectural choices (windowed local/global split vs. full attention, RoPE jittering, choice of G windows/patch sizes, omission of the Gram loss, iBOT masking ratio changes) are largely absent; the only reported ablation (Table 7) is limited to optimizer/crop-size choices on a single fold of one segmentation dataset, so the paper's central architectural claims are asserted rather than empirically isolated.

Pretraining data composition is heavily skewed toward chest CT (NLST alone contributes >50% of SSL data), which the authors acknowledge likely explains stronger lung-related performance and weaker abdominal performance — a limitation that tempers the "general-purpose foundation model" framing.

No comparison of computational cost/efficiency (FLOPs, memory, throughput) against baselines despite the paper's framing around making 3D attention "computationally tractable"; the actual savings of the two-stage design versus a plain ViT baseline are asserted analytically (Eq. 4) but never empirically measured.

Code repository link is left blank ("Code available at:"), and several implementation details relevant to reproducibility (e.g., exact window configuration at various resolutions, full LLM-rewrite prompt/pipeline validation) are deferred to supplementary material without independent verification of rewrite quality/bias.

The qualitative saliency maps (Fig. 4) and segmentation examples (Fig. 6) are described as curated/non-curated inconsistently and are not accompanied by any quantitative localization metric, limiting their evidentiary value for the claimed clinical relevance of representations.

strengths: Comprehensive systems contribution: a full end-to-end pipeline including a novel two-stage local/global ViT architecture with 3D RoPE tailored to CT anisotropy, a two-stage DINOv3+iBOT+KoLeo SSL pretraining scheme, and a SigLIP-based vision-language alignment stage adapted for noisy many-to-many clinical text.

Large-scale, exclusively open-data pretraining corpus (229,619 CT series across 8 public sources) with detailed, well-documented preprocessing and filtering criteria, supporting reproducibility and community reuse.

Broad downstream evaluation spanning three distinct task families (frozen-embedding biomarker classification against 10 competing foundation models, semantic segmentation against 8 conv/transformer baselines, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval against 4 baselines), which is unusually thorough for a foundation-model paper.

Encoder-only segmentation adaptation (SEoMT) is a clean, decoder-agnostic way to isolate representation quality, and the associated ablations (optimizer choice, crop size, SSL vs. VLA initialization) are informative and transparently reported, including a negative/mixed result (SGD divergence).

Honest reporting of a case where the model underperforms a strong baseline (Merlin on Findings-only retrieval), and provision of confidence intervals for the biomarker benchmark, which strengthens the credibility of the claims made.

Extensive supplementary material detailing hardware, hyperparameters, dataset composition, and qualitative visualizations (saliency maps, UMAP), aiding reproducibility despite the very large compute budget used.
weaknesses: Potential train/test leakage is not addressed: AMOS CT scans are listed as part of the SSL pretraining corpus (Table 4, 2,450 scans) while AMOS22-CT (300 labeled volumes) is also used as a downstream segmentation evaluation benchmark; the paper does not state whether these labeled evaluation cases were excluded from pretraining, which undermines the validity of the AMOS segmentation comparison if overlap exists.

Segmentation results are mixed relative to strong convolutional baselines: plain nnU-Net outperforms SPECTRE on AMOS-CT (88.87 vs 87.55) and nnU-Net ResEnc L outperforms it on KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD; the Discussion section's framing ("surpasses all other domain-specific transformer-based models") is accurate only relative to transformer baselines and could be read as overstating the overall standing versus conv-based SOTA.

The method combines many design choices (DINO+iBOT+KoLeo weighting, omission of the Gram loss, RoPE-box jittering, local/global window split, masking ratio range) but most of these are justified only qualitatively; there is essentially no ablation isolating the individual contribution of each pretraining component or architectural choice (only the segmentation-side optimizer/crop-size ablation is provided).

Text-to-image retrieval performance is inconsistent: SPECTRE trails Merlin substantially on Findings-section retrieval (e.g., Recall@1, N=32: 55.5% vs 77.6%), which is a non-trivial gap for a paper claiming state-of-the-art cross-modal alignment; the discussion attributes this to text augmentation robustness but offers no controlled experiment isolating that cause.

The "open" framing is partially inconsistent with the pretraining pipeline, since radiology report paraphrasing relies on a closed-source, proprietary LLM (Gemini 2 Flash) for data augmentation—an external dependency not disclosed as a limitation.

Pretraining requires a very large industrial cluster (24 B200 GPUs, ~4.3TB combined GPU memory), which, despite the promised code release, raises practical reproducibility concerns for most academic groups; the code repository link is left blank in the submitted manuscript.

Hyperparameters for the segmentation pipeline were tuned solely on KiTS23 fold-0 and then applied uniformly to all other datasets/folds; while this avoids optimism on KiTS23, it does not establish that the same hyperparameters are near-optimal for the other three datasets, and no dataset-specific tuning or sensitivity analysis is reported.

No variance/significance reporting is given for the segmentation Dice results in Table 1 (unlike the biomarker classification results, which include 95% CIs), making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements over Primus or nnU-Net are statistically meaningful.

strengths: Comprehensive engineering effort: the paper combines a carefully designed local-global 3D ViT architecture (windowed local attention + global aggregation, 3D RoPE with jittering) with a two-stage DINOv3-style SSL + SigLIP VLA pretraining pipeline, and describes hyperparameters, hardware, and data curation in substantial detail, aiding reproducibility.

The pretraining corpus (229k series from 8 public datasets) is entirely open, and the authors commit to releasing code, which is valuable for the community compared to many closed-data CT foundation models.

Broad and fairly rigorous evaluation across three task families (biomarker classification via frozen kNN, semantic segmentation via encoder-only SEoMT integrated into nnU-Net, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval), with confidence intervals, saliency maps, decoder ablations, and robustness checks (text dropout, spacing robustness) that go beyond a single headline metric.

Reasonable comparisons against many strong baselines (11 CT foundation models for biomarker prediction, several transformer segmentation backbones, CT-CLIP/Merlin/OpenCLIP/BioMedCLIP for retrieval), and honest reporting of cases where SPECTRE does not win (e.g., CT-FM on TotalSegmentator, Merlin on Findings retrieval, NSCLC-Radiogenomics/Colorectal-Liver-Metastases AUC).

The decoder ablation (Linear vs SEoMT vs UNETR) is a self-critical analysis showing the limits of the encoder-only evaluation protocol and clarifying that reported segmentation numbers likely underestimate the encoder's true capability.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'consistently outperforming prior CT foundation models' is only partially supported: SPECTRE wins on 4/6 biomarker tasks (with large CIs on 2 of the 4 losing tasks suggesting weak separation), underperforms CT-FM on TotalSegmentator variants, and underperforms Merlin substantially on Findings-to-image retrieval; the abstract/discussion framing is more triumphant than the results warrant.

No ablation isolating the contribution of individual architectural choices proposed as central contributions (windowed local+global attention design, RoPE jittering, anisotropic tokenization) against simpler baselines (e.g., plain 3D ViT, standard non-anisotropic patches) — the paper asserts these choices are necessary but provides no controlled comparison demonstrating their necessity versus the specific SSL/VLA recipe or larger data/compute budget being the actual driver of gains.

The comparisons across the 11 foundation models in Fig.1/Fig.3 and Tab.2/3 are not fully matched in training data, model size, or compute; it is unclear how much of SPECTRE's advantage stems from architectural novelty versus simply larger, more carefully curated pretraining data and far larger compute budget (24 B200 GPUs) than most baselines had access to, which confounds the paper's central architectural claims.

The paper does not report standard errors/uncertainty for the main Fig.1 radar comparison in the main text (only in supplementary Fig.3), and does not perform statistical significance testing for the '4/6 wins' claim, making it hard to assess whether the differences are meaningful versus noise for datasets with small sample sizes (e.g., 133-194 patients).

Some technical/architectural claims are asserted without ablation evidence in the main text, e.g., the omission of the DINOv3 Gram loss is justified qualitatively ('relatively narrow operational spectrum of the CT domain') without an experiment showing it would hurt or help.

The SEoMT segmentation results, while competitive, are consistently below the strongest baselines (nnU-Net ResEnc L, CT-FM) on several benchmarks, and the paper's own decoder ablation (Table 10) shows a substantially weaker detection rate for small lesions than nnU-Net ResEnc L, somewhat undermining the practical significance of segmentation results despite honest self-reporting.

The manuscript is dense and reads partly as a technical report; some notation (e.g., Eq. 15's D term, some symbol reuse) is imprecise or could be clarified, and heavy reliance on supplementary material makes the main paper less self-contained.

No comparison to very recent large multimodal 2D/3D medical foundation models beyond the specific chosen 11 baselines, and no discussion of computational cost/inference efficiency trade-offs of the two-stage local/global architecture versus simpler single-stage ViT baselines at equivalent parameter counts.

strengths: Substantial engineering effort with a large, fully open-data pretraining corpus (~230K CT series) and transparent documentation of data curation, filtering, and preprocessing across 8 public datasets.

Reasonably principled architectural adaptations for volumetric data: anisotropic 3D patch embeddings, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style scale jittering, and a two-stage local/global attention scheme that keeps quadratic attention cost tractable for large 3D token counts.

Broad evaluation protocol spanning three distinct task families (frozen-embedding biomarker classification, dense semantic segmentation via an EoMT-style encoder-only decoder, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval), compared against a large and relevant set of 11 prior CT foundation models.

Extensive and generally honest supplementary ablations (optimizer choice, crop size, decoder complexity, text corruption robustness, spacing robustness), including analyses that reveal limitations (e.g., poor small-lesion detection) rather than hiding them.

Clear, mathematically detailed presentation of the SSL (DINO/iBOT/KoLeo) and VLA (SigLIP) objectives and of the tokenization/attention mechanisms, aiding reproducibility together with the stated intent to release code and weights.
weaknesses: The abstract's claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' is not well supported by the paper's own results: nnU-Net ResEnc L (a non-foundation-model, task-specific baseline) beats SPECTRE on all three segmentation datasets in Table 1, and CT-FM beats SPECTRE on 2 of 3 TotalSegmentator benchmarks (Table 9), and Merlin substantially outperforms SPECTRE on Findings-to-image retrieval (Table 3).

The decoder ablation (Table 10) shows that the proposed SEoMT head performs poorly on small (<10mm) lesion detection (5.36% vs. 22.79% for nnU-Net ResEnc L), undermining confidence that the pretrained representation captures fine-grained spatial detail needed for clinically important small structures; the paper's window-level mean-pooling into a single descriptor plausibly discards spatial information that would matter for such targets.

Segmentation baselines in Table 1 (CoTr, nnFormer, SwinUNETRv2, UNETR, WaveFormer, Primus) are taken directly from a different paper (Wald et al.) rather than re-run under the authors' exact protocol, raising concerns about strict comparability (training budgets, folds, hyperparameter tuning may differ).

The technical contribution is largely a careful integration/adaptation of existing components (DINOv3, SigLIP, RoPE, EoMT) to 3D CT rather than a fundamentally new method; the paper does not clearly isolate which specific design choices (vs. simply more data/compute) drive the reported gains.

Reported performance gains on biomarker classification are only achieved on 4/6 tasks, and per the supplementary confidence intervals, some of these differences may not be statistically robust given small dataset sizes noted by the authors themselves.

Reproducibility is nontrivial in practice despite open data/code: pretraining requires 24 B200 GPUs, which is a substantial barrier for independent verification even though the underlying data is public.

The zero-shot retrieval comparison to MedSigLIP is somewhat unfair/strawman-like, since that baseline's poor performance is attributed to a 128-token input limit truncating reports, making the comparison less informative about representation quality per se.

Key quantitative results for the biomarker benchmark are presented primarily via radar plots (Fig. 1) in the main text rather than tables with exact numbers, making precise comparison across models harder for readers (numeric values only appear via bar charts with CIs in the supplement).

strengths: Trains exclusively on large-scale open CT data (229,619 series across 8 public datasets), addressing an important gap since many competing CT foundation models rely on private data; this improves reproducibility and community access.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct task families (biomarker classification via kNN on 6 datasets, semantic segmentation on 6+ benchmarks including KiTS23/LiTS/WORD/TotalSegmentator, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE/Merlin), compared against a wide set of 11 prior CT foundation models and multiple segmentation architectures.

Well-motivated architectural adaptations for volumetric CT (anisotropic 3D patch embedding matching typical CT voxel spacing ratios, two-stage local/global attention to make full-scan attention tractable, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style scale jittering) with clear complexity/engineering justification.

Thorough supplementary material: detailed dataset curation/filtering criteria, training hyperparameters, hardware specs, and multiple informative ablations (optimizer choice, crop size, decoder variants including a Linear vs SEoMT vs UNETR comparison with small-lesion detection-rate analysis).

Honest discussion of limitations (thoracic-heavy pretraining corpus, degraded performance on small lesions with the lightweight SEoMT decoder, noise in clinical reports) rather than overselling every result.

Practical VLA design choices addressing known 3D-specific issues, e.g., SigLIP loss to handle many-to-many image-report pairs and small effective batch sizes, and LLM-based report paraphrasing (LaCLIP-style) to combat report noise, with supporting robustness ablations (token/span dropout, report length).
weaknesses: The abstract's claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' is not fully supported: it wins on only 4/6 biomarker tasks (with wide, low-power confidence intervals on the 2 tasks it loses), is clearly beaten by CT-FM on TSv2-Full/TSv2-Merlin segmentation, and is substantially outperformed by Merlin on Findings-based retrieval (e.g., 55.5% vs 77.6% Recall@1 at N=32) despite the paper's framing implying broad superiority.

Segmentation gains over strong baselines are numerically small (e.g., 86.64% vs Primus-L's 86.04%, vs. nnU-Net ResEnc L's 88.06% on KiTS23) and no statistical significance test is reported, making it hard to assess whether the encoder actually provides a meaningful improvement over existing transformer backbones for this task.

The main paper presents no ablation isolating the individual contribution of the SSL (DINO) stage vs. the VLA (SigLIP) stage vs. the local/global two-stage attention design on the primary headline results (biomarker prediction, retrieval); most architectural justification is qualitative rather than empirically validated component-by-component.

Code/model release links are left blank in both the main text and supplementary ('Code available at:', GitHub link left empty), so reproducibility cannot currently be verified despite this being emphasized as a core contribution.

Pretraining requires an unusually large industrial compute budget (24 B200 GPUs across 3 DGX systems), which is not clearly discussed in terms of comparability/fairness to baselines trained with far less compute, and no compute-normalized comparison or efficiency benchmarking (throughput/memory vs. baselines) is provided despite 'efficient' being part of the architectural framing.

The SEoMT segmentation decoder is shown in the paper's own ablation (Table 10) to substantially underperform a more conventional UNETR-style decoder, especially on small lesions (detection rate 1.53% vs 11.12%), which somewhat undercuts the narrative that the encoder-only representation is a strong drop-in for dense prediction tasks without more decoder engineering.
